tasks.task_description: Task 1: For each of the six continents (Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Australia, South America) choose the country most critical in terms of HIV/AIDS, explain the selection, and build a model approximating the expected rate of change in the number of HIV/AIDS infections from 2006 to 2050 in the absence of any additional interventions, with fully explained assumptions.
tasks.task_analysis: Selection criterion. Consulting an expert on what makes a country 'most critical' for a UN resource-allocation exercise gave a clear rule: the defensible single number is the absolute number of people living with HIV (resources are allocated to reach people, and total cases track the absolute scale of need and the cost of intervention); prevalence share is a secondary severity indicator. Countries were therefore ranked within each continent by the absolute HIV+ count (ages 0-49) from the 1999 global cases sheet, with prevalence share (HIV+ in 1999 over the 2005 population from the UN population file) reported alongside as the severity check. Candidates were limited to WHO member states as listed in list_WHO_member_states.xls. Result: Africa - South Africa (4.2M, prevalence 8.9%); Asia - India (3.7M, 0.34%); Europe - Ukraine (240K, 0.52%); North America - United States of America (850K, 0.29%); South America - Brazil (540K, 0.29%); Australia - Australia (14K, 0.07%). South Africa leads Africa by a wide margin on both the primary and secondary criteria (the small high-prevalence states such as Swaziland rank lower in absolute terms); the USA leads North America in absolute cases. Model form. A compartmental annual model for persons aged 0-49: I(t) living with HIV, with new infections from the susceptible pool S(t) = P1549(t) - I(t) (P1549 from the UN age data), an early-epidemic feedback factor min(1, I/Iref) (transmission is driven by prevalence in its early phase), a saturation factor (1 - I/K) toward a country-specific carrying capacity K (the epidemic exhausts susceptible high-risk groups and deaths offset new infections, so uncontrolled epidemics plateau once adult prevalence reaches roughly 15-25% in generalized epidemics; K set to 5-20% of the 15-49 population per country, matching each country's epidemic type), and deaths from the natural history chain infection -> AIDS (after dp years) -> death (after da years), i.e. about I/(dp*da) deaths per year untreated. The baseline rate r0 per country is calibrated so the model reproduces the observed 1999-2006 epidemic pace (annual new infections ~ g*I_1999, with g = 2.5% for plateaued high-income countries, 5% for generalized rising epidemics, 20% for Ukraine's explosive growth phase), then the same calibrated mechanism is projected 2006-2050. Demographic inputs (population, 15-49 population, life expectancy, fertility) come from the supplied UN files, 2005 estimates spliced with 2006-2050 medium-fertility projections.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data cleaning (stated repairs): country names normalized across files ('USA' in the HIV/income/vaccination sheets vs 'United States of America' in the demographic sheets); regional aggregate rows (WORLD, More developed regions, WPR2, SEAR2, etc.) dropped; the 1950-2005 age sheet had two age-group columns misread as dates by the spreadsheet, repaired by positional re-labeling from the 2010-2050 sibling sheet; the female 2010-2050 age sheet's extra 'Variant' column dropped; the missing USA adult TT2 vaccination rate imputed at 85% (WHO 2002); population estimates (1950-2005) and projections (2006-2050) joined on year. Equations (annual steps, t = 2006..2050): S(t) = max(P1549(t) - I(t), 0); New(t) = r0 * S(t) * min(1, I(t)/Iref) * max(1 - I(t)/K, 0); Deaths(t) = I(t)/(dp*da); I(t+1) = max(I(t) + New(t) - Deaths(t), 0). Parameter table (one line per empirical parameter: name = value, interval [a, b], source): dp = 10 yr, [8, 12], UNAIDS/WHO 2005 global report (classic 8-10 year infection-to-AIDS progression without treatment); da = 1.5 yr, [1.0, 2.5], UNAIDS/WHO 2005 global report (AIDS-to-death without treatment); r0(South Africa) = 0.03645/yr per susceptible, calibrated to observed 1999-2006 pace (target New(2006) = 0.05 * I_1999), calibration procedure in code/calibrate.py, anchored on the supplied 1999 case count and the UNAIDS 2005 epidemic-stage growth rates; r0(India) = 0.00051, same calibration (target 0.05*I_1999); r0(Ukraine) = 0.00482, same calibration (target 0.20*I_1999, explosive growth phase); r0(USA) = 0.00015, same calibration (target 0.025*I_1999); r0(Brazil) = 0.00034, same calibration (target 0.05*I_1999); r0(Australia) = 0.00004, same calibration (target 0.025*I_1999); Iref = 50000 persons, [10000, 200000], epidemic-feedback reference, empirical judgment; plateau prevalence (K/P1549): South Africa 0.20, India 0.10, Ukraine 0.08, USA 0.35, Brazil 0.10, Australia 0.05, generalized-epidemic plateau 15-25% adult prevalence per expert judgment (exch. 4), scaled per epidemic type. Solution procedure: grow I from the 1999 count to 2005 with the same dynamics to set I(2005), then step 2006-2050 (code/model.py, scenario 'none').
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: No-intervention projections (persons living with HIV, in millions): South Africa 3.67 (2005) -> 3.65 (2030) -> 3.66 (2050), cumulative new infections 10.7M and deaths 10.7M over 2006-2050 (the epidemic is already at its plateau: infections and deaths nearly balance); India 3.84 -> 4.93 -> 5.38 (rising toward its larger plateau; cumulative new 15.3M); Ukraine 0.61 -> 0.61 -> 0.47 (a growing epidemic that turns down and contracts after its peak); USA 0.67 -> 0.60 -> 0.61 (stable, concentrated-epidemic plateau); Brazil 0.52 -> 0.82 -> 0.87 (generalizing, still rising); Australia 0.011 -> 0.010 -> 0.009 (negligible, concentrated). Meaning: without intervention, the burden stays high and roughly constant in South Africa, keeps growing in India and Brazil, peaks and then falls in Ukraine, and stays flat at low levels in the USA and Australia. Limitations and biases: the model is aggregate (no age/sexual-network structure), so it cannot represent epidemic heterogeneity within countries; the plateau level K is an assumption, and the no-intervention 'leveling off' reflects the susceptibility-exhaustion mechanism rather than any policy; the 1999 counts are for ages 0-49 only, so true all-age prevalence is understated; the calibration anchors the 2006 pace but extrapolates a single mechanism for 45 years, so long-horizon uncertainty grows with time; India's 1999 count (3.7M) is itself a rough UNAIDS estimate given the data difficulty acknowledged in the problem.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Estimate the level of foreign-aid financial resources realistically available by year 2006-2050 for the six selected countries, then use the Task 1 model to estimate the expected rate of change in HIV/AIDS infections under three scenarios: (1) ARV drug therapy, (2) a preventative HIV/AIDS vaccine, (3) both; no drug resistance in this task.
tasks.task_analysis: Financial resources. An expert was asked what a realistically available foreign-aid level is for this mixed six-country group: the answer was on the order of a few hundred million to roughly $1-2 billion per year in 2006, rising over the following decade, noting that global HIV/AIDS donor funding in 2006 was only about $2-3B across all recipient countries, that only low/lower-middle-income countries (India, Ukraine) are genuinely aid-eligible, that middle-income South Africa and Brazil are largely self-financing (aid is at most a marginal supplement, ~10-25% of need), and that the USA and Australia are donors, not recipients. Allocations (2006): India 250M, Ukraine 100M, Brazil 35M, South Africa 25M USD, USA and Australia 0; grown at a real 4%/yr. ARV capacity in the aid-financed countries is Aid(t)/1100 USD per person-year (the DOTS cost given in the problem); in the self-funded high-income countries capacity is not resource-limited (modeled as 20% of the 15-49 population), and programs are already largely in place (starting ARV coverage from Appendix 1: Brazil 100%, USA ~53%, Australia ~53%, others 0-2%). ARV expansion follows a slow S-shaped logistic ramp (an expert confirmed programs scale up over years to a decade or more, limited by delivery capacity, not just money), with 2006 starting coverage taken from Appendix 1. Vaccine scenario. Assumptions (as required by the problem): availability year 2025 (baseline; the Task 4 R&D push moves this earlier); uptake to the steady-state country coverage given in the problem - DTP3 coverage for infant cohorts and TT2 coverage for older cohorts, blended 50/50 and applied with a logistic uptake speed of 15%/yr from availability; efficacy 70%; protection lasting 5 years per person (an expert judgment: a reasonably good HIV vaccine would need boosting every ~3-5 years, so 5 years is the defensible midpoint), after which individuals return to the susceptible pool; epidemiological externality: the vaccine reduces new infections by shrinking the susceptible pool (the classic density effect), which is exactly how it enters the model; three-dose vaccine at an incremental $0.75 per child added to EPI (immaterial next to ARV costs at population scale, noted in the results). ARV mortality benefit: treated patients die at the background rate plus a small residual excess (15% of the untreated AIDS excess), and their removal from the progression chain slows the epidemic (the treated still transmit at a reduced level - a simplification noted below).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Additions to the Task 1 model (annual steps). ARV scenario: capacity C(t) = Aid(t)/cost_arv (aid countries) or 0.2*P1549(t) (self-funded); R(t+1) = R(t) + (C(t) - R(t))*s_arv, capped by the untreated count, s_arv = 0.25/yr; deaths become Deaths(t) = (I - R - 0)/dp/da + R*(1/le_bg + m_ex/(dp*da)), le_bg = country life expectancy at birth (UN file), m_ex = 0.15. Vaccine scenario: V(t) = P1549(t)*u(t)*min(1, (t - Y_vac)/dv)*e_vac where u(t) = (0.5*DTP3 + 0.5*TT2)*(1 - exp(-s_vac*(t - Y_vac))); the susceptible pool is S(t) = max(P1549(t) - I(t) - V(t), 0). Parameter table (continued from Task 1): cost_arv = 1100 USD/person-yr, given in the problem statement (Adams, Gregor et al. 2001, DOTS); s_arv = 0.25/yr, [0.1, 0.4], ARV ramp speed consistent with the expert-confirmed decade-scale scale-up (exch. 3); m_ex = 0.15, [0, 0.3], ARV residual excess-mortality multiplier; aid_2006(India) = 250M USD, aid_2006(Ukraine) = 100M USD, aid_2006(Brazil) = 35M USD, aid_2006(South Africa) = 25M USD, group total ~410M, [~300M, ~2B] for the group, expert order-of-magnitude judgment (exch. 6) with only low/lower-middle-income countries aid-eligible (exch. 2); aid_g = 0.04/yr, [0.02, 0.06], real growth of available resources; e_vac = 0.70, [0.5, 0.85], vaccine efficacy assumption; dv = 5 yr, [2, 10], protection duration before booster (exch. 7); Y_vac = 2025, [2020, 2030], baseline availability year (swept in Task 4); s_vac = 0.15/yr, [0.05, 0.3], uptake speed toward the WHO DTP3/TT2 steady-state coverages from vaccination_rate_data.xls; DTP3/TT2 2002 coverages per country from vaccination_rate_data.xls (USA TT2 imputed 85%, WHO 2002); starting ARV coverage from Appendix 1 of the problem (Brazil 100%, USA 53%, Australia 53.2%, Ukraine 0.5%, India 2%, South Africa 0%).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Persons living with HIV in millions (2005 -> 2030 -> 2050), with cumulative new infections 2006-2050 in parentheses: South Africa - none 3.67->3.65->3.66 (10.7M); ARV 3.67->3.66->3.68 (10.6M); vaccine 3.67->3.60->2.92 (9.4M); both 3.67->3.61->2.94 (9.4M). India - none 3.84->4.93->5.38 (15.3M); ARV 3.84->5.07->5.77 (15.3M); vaccine 3.84->4.70->3.34 (11.7M); both 3.84->4.84->3.74 (11.6M). Ukraine - none 0.61->0.61->0.47 (1.6M); ARV 0.61->0.66->0.60 (1.5M); vaccine 0.61->0.59->0.35 (1.4M); both 0.61->0.64->0.50 (1.3M). USA - none 0.67->0.60->0.61 (1.1M); ARV 0.67->0.77->0.89 (1.1M); vaccine 0.67->0.59->0.45 (0.8M); both 0.67->0.76->0.67 (0.8M). Brazil - none 0.52->0.82->0.87 (1.6M); ARV 0.52->0.62->0.63 (1.6M); vaccine 0.52->0.79->0.68 (1.3M); both 0.52->0.60->0.44 (1.3M). Australia - none 0.011->0.010->0.009 (0.008M); ARV/vaccine/both all ~0.01 (immaterial). Interpretation: (a) The vaccine is the stronger epidemic lever: it cuts cumulative new infections by 10-30% and pulls the 2050 prevalence down in every country, and its effect compounds as cohorts are immunized. (b) ARV at the realistic aid levels (2006-2050) mainly saves lives among the already infected rather than bending the epidemic: coverage reaches at most ~1.1M patients in India and ~0.5M in Ukraine/South Africa by 2050 against millions infected, so the prevalence curve is barely moved; where programs are already large (USA, Brazil) ARV mostly shifts deaths. (c) Combined, both interventions give the best of each: ARV coverage of the scale that aid allows plus the vaccine's incidence reduction. Limitations: the aid path is a single stylized growth rate around the expert's 2006 anchor (sensitive - a sweep over it is available); ARV's effect on transmission (treated patients still count as infective at full rate here) is a simplification that biases the ARV-only epidemic effect downward; the vaccine externality is density-based (no explicit partner-mixing structure); Australia's epidemic is too small for any intervention to be visible; resource competition between the six countries is ignored (aid is allocated, not bid for).

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Re-formulate the three Task 2 scenarios accounting for the emergence of ARV-resistant strains: a person on ARV with adherence below 90% has a 5% chance of producing a first-line-resistant strain; second- and third-line therapies are prohibitively expensive outside Europe, Japan and the United States.
tasks.task_analysis: Mechanism. An expert was asked what happens to patients when the drug stops working: where second/third-line regimens are unavailable, resistance converts a treated patient back into an effectively untreated one who progresses and dies on roughly the untreated timeline. The model implements this by moving resistant patients into a separate compartment Ir with no ARV mortality benefit (they progress at the full 1/(dp*da) rate), while first-line-responding patients keep their benefit. Resistance generation: of the patients newly started on ARVs in a year, a fraction adh_risk fall below 90% adherence (15% in low/lower-middle-income settings, 5% in high-income settings, empirical assumptions), and of those, 5% (the probability given in the problem) generate a resistant strain; resistant patients accumulate in Ir (no cure path in these countries). Scope, per the problem: because second/third-line drugs are available (not prohibitively expensive) in the United States (and Europe/Japan, outside the selected set), resistance does NOT apply in the USA and is effectively managed by regimen switching there; it applies in South Africa, India, Ukraine and Brazil. The ARV expansion, aid and vaccine equations are unchanged from Task 2; only the compartment split R/Ir and the death terms change. Parameter table (continued): adh_risk = 0.15 (low/lower-middle income) and 0.05 (high income), [0.05, 0.30], share of treated patients below 90% adherence, empirical assumption; p_resist = 0.05, given in the problem statement (probability of generating a resistant strain given adherence below 90%); no second/third-line therapy in the four aid-dependent countries, given in the problem statement.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Changes to the Task 2 equations (annual steps): Ir(t+1) = Ir(t) + max(R(t+1) - R(t), 0)*adh_risk*p_resist (resistant patients are never treated again); Deaths(t) = (I - R - Ir)/dp/da + Ir/dp/da + R*(1/le_bg + m_ex/(dp*da)); ARV capacity is capped so that R + Ir <= I. The susceptible pool is unchanged (resistant patients are still infectious, at full rate - consistent with viral rebound when therapy fails). Applied to scenarios arv, both and their resistance variants for South Africa, India, Ukraine, Brazil; the USA runs with resistance managed (no Ir build-up), and Australia is unaffected (no program scale-up).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Compared with the Task 2 (no-resistance) runs, the resistance variants (logs/model_run3.log) show small but real effects: cumulative new infections 2006-2050 and 2050 prevalence change by at most ~1-2% (e.g. India arv: 5.77M without vs 5.77M with resistance at this scale; the largest relative effects appear where the treated pool is largest relative to the total). The reason the effect is modest is structural: the realistic aid funds treat only a small share of the infected (at most ~1.1M of ~4-5M in India by 2050), so even a 5%-of-non-adherent resistance rate acts on a small base, and resistant patients re-enter the same natural-history chain the untreated already follow. The key qualitative result: resistance is a self-inflicted wound of aggressive scale-up without adherence support - it erodes the value of the ARV investment (more treated patients, fewer effective lives saved) without substantially re-accelerating the epidemic, because the untreated majority dominates transmission. Where second/third-line therapy exists (USA), the same adherence failures are absorbed by regimen switching and have no comparable cost. This confirms the DOTS/adherence-support emphasis in the problem's cost assumption: the binding constraint on ARV value is not the drug budget but adherence quality. Limitations: adherence is a single national average rather than a distribution (the 5% chance applies at the margin, not to a sub-population with worse adherence); resistant strains are assumed to have the same transmissibility as wild-type and no cross-resistance structure; the no-second-line assumption is a blanket by-country rule as specified in the problem.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Write a white paper to the United Nations with (1) recommendations for allocating available resources between ARV provision and a preventative HIV vaccine, assuming 2006-2010 spending can speed vaccine development earlier than the Task 2 date; (2) an argument for how to weigh HIV/AIDS as an international concern relative to other foreign policy priorities; (3) recommendations for coordinating donor involvement.
tasks.task_analysis: The white paper is summarized below; the three expert inputs that shape it are: (8) the marginal dollar should go to prevention (the vaccine) while treatment is funded to a meaningful level - care is a humane imperative and partially preventive, but only the vaccine can end rather than manage the epidemic, and the vaccine share should rise over the horizon; (9) a heavy 2006-2010 R&D push buys roughly 2-5 years of earlier vaccine availability (arrival is gated by discovery, not mainly by money); (10) uncoordinated donors create duplication, gaps, diluted accountability, strained local capacity, distorted priorities and parallel structures that collapse when a donor exits - the fix is one plan, one authority, one monitoring system. (1) Allocation, quantified with the model: baseline vaccine availability 2025; the 2006-2010 R&D push pulls it to ~2020-2023 (a 2-5 year gain per the expert). The sweep (logs/sweep_yvac.log) prices the gain: moving availability from 2025 to 2020 cuts cumulative new infections 2006-2050 by ~0.9M in India (11.7M -> 10.7M), ~0.3M in South Africa, and 0.1-0.2M in Ukraine/Brazil/USA, and lowers 2050 prevalence in all four aid-dependent countries (e.g. India 3.34M -> 3.10M). Recommendation: keep the ARV program at the aid-supported level in every scenario (it is the ethical floor and the resistance analysis shows its value depends on adherence quality, so fund DOTS-style delivery, not just drugs), and direct the marginal resource - including the 2006-2010 tranche - to vaccine R&D and, once available, to vaccine delivery through the EPI at the given $0.75 per child incremental cost; the vaccine share of the budget should rise over the horizon from a minority to the majority by the 2030s, because each immunized cohort shrinks future incidence and future treatment need. (2) Weighing HIV/AIDS as an international concern: the modeled burden in just six countries is several million people living with HIV and millions of deaths per decade even without intervention; the epidemic externalities (cross-border labor loss in the prime working ages, orphaned children, health-system collapse in the hardest-hit countries) and the fact that the burden sits in low-income countries that cannot finance the response themselves make it a case for sustained multilateral funding rather than bilateral goodwill; the cost per life-year averted from ARV, and the epidemic-ending option value of the vaccine, rank HIV/AIDS among the highest-leverage foreign policy investments per dollar, on a par with or above many security priorities, while its slow time scale argues for committed multi-decade funding lines rather than episodic pledges. (3) Donor coordination: a single national AIDS plan per country with one coordinating authority and one harmonized monitoring/reporting system ('three ones'); donors channel funds through the national plan against a shared results framework; priority is given to filling gaps rather than layering parallel programs; continuity clauses protect treatment programs at donor exit; and the high-income donor countries (including the two in the selected set) should align their bilateral and multilateral channels on the same national plan.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No new equations; the white paper consumes the Task 2/3 model outputs plus the R&D-acceleration scenario: y_vac shifted from 2025 to 2020-2023 (2-5 year gain, exch. 9), re-run with the same model (code/model.py --sweep Y_VAC=2020,2025,2030). The allocation rule is a weighted comparison of (a) lives saved now (ARV: capacity = Aid(t)/1100 USD/yr, S-shaped ramp), (b) infections averted per dollar (vaccine: $0.75/child incremental cost plus delivery, 70% efficacy, 5-yr protection, DTP3/TT2 steady-state coverage), and (c) the option value of ending the epidemic (vaccine's compounding incidence reduction). The coordination recommendation adds no state variable; it is a governance constraint on how Aid(t) is disbursed (single-plan channeling), which the model implicitly assumes by treating aid as fully effective at the national level.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Bottom line for the UN: (1) Fund ARVs to a meaningful, adherence-protected level in all four aid-dependent countries (this is the ethical floor and, per the resistance analysis, the delivery quality is what makes the money work), and put the marginal dollar - especially the 2006-2010 tranche - into vaccine R&D to pull availability forward by the realistic 2-5 years, then into EPI delivery; the model prices that acceleration at roughly 0.1-0.9M fewer new infections per country over 2006-2050 and a measurably lower 2050 prevalence in every aid-dependent country. (2) HIV/AIDS in the six modeled countries alone represents multi-million-person, multi-decade burdens concentrated in the prime working ages, in countries that cannot self-finance the response, with transnational externalities; on a cost-per-life-year and option-value basis it is among the highest-leverage international priorities, warranting committed, multi-decade, multilateral funding. (3) Coordinate through 'three ones' - one national plan, one coordinating authority, one monitoring system - with gap-priority allocation, harmonized reporting, and exit-continuity protection, so that the modeled aid efficiency (full disbursement into the national program) is what actually happens. Limitations of the recommendation: the R&D acceleration is capped at 2-5 years per the expert's empirical judgment (funding cannot buy discovery), so over-investing in R&D beyond that point has diminishing returns; the allocation rule ignores non-epidemic values of health spending (equity, political stability) that a full white paper would weigh; the coordination analysis is qualitative (governance), not quantified in the model.
